definition: Made shorter by having a part cut off, especially the end.
example: The truncated version of the speech left out its most moving final paragraph.
nuance: Truncated suggests an abrupt cut, often at the end, while abridged implies careful condensing that keeps the essentials.
prompt: A student's essay file was damaged while it was being uploaded.
options: The truncated file stopped mid-sentence, missing the last two pages.
The truncated file had grown to twice its original length after the upload.
The truncated file was complete, but every letter had been scrambled into symbols.
The truncated file now appeared in Spanish instead of the original English.
reasons: Losing the ending so the text breaks off abruptly is exactly what this word describes.
Truncation removes material, so a file that doubled in size is the opposite.
Garbled characters in a complete file describe corruption, not a missing portion.
Changing the language is translation; nothing has been cut off.

practice.prompt: A radio station had to end its live concert broadcast early.
options: The truncated broadcast was full of static, though every song aired in full.
The truncated broadcast played every song in full, just at a faster tempo.
Listeners got a truncated broadcast that ended before the final song.
The truncated broadcast ran an extra hour so the band could play encores.
reasons: Poor sound quality with nothing missing is not a shortening at all.
Speeding up keeps all the content, while this word requires a part to be removed.
A program cut off before its planned finish has been shortened abruptly.
Running longer than planned is the reverse of being cut short.
